Pile cap
Placed under an individual column: a reinforced concrete block distributes the column load to the pile group below it. The pile reinforcement is anchored into the cap.
Grillage (pile grillage)
Under walls and rows of columns: the pile heads are tied together by reinforced concrete beams, and the load of the wall reaches the piles through the beam.
Slab (piled raft)
Under large, uniformly loaded buildings – for example towers and underground car parks: the reinforced concrete slab works together with the piles and also transfers load to the soil.

Quiz – what is a deep foundation?
What fundamentally distinguishes a deep foundation from a shallow foundation?
Besides its base, it can also transfer load to the soil along its shaft (side).
It always reaches at least 10 m deep.
It can only be made of precast elements.
It needs no structure tying its heads together.
A deep foundation is a load-transferring element between the structure and the deeper bearing stratum that transfers load at its base and along its shaft.
Which is NOT a typical reason for a deep foundation?
The bearing stratum is directly below ground level.
A shallow foundation would produce unacceptable settlement.
There is a risk of scour around the bridge pier.
The reliable bearing stratum lies only deeper.
If the good layer is directly below the surface, a shallow foundation is usually the simplest and cheapest solution.
What are the three main types of deep foundation?
Pile foundations, diaphragm wall foundations, well and box foundations
Strip foundations, rafts, pile foundations
CFA, Franki pile, jet grouting
Soil replacement, preloading, piling
Today pile foundations are built most often; diaphragm walls are used mainly for excavation support, and well and box foundations are increasingly rare.
What is an excavated block foundation?
A transitional solution: a block excavated without support and concreted immediately, in cohesive soil to approx. 5–6 m.
A precast reinforced concrete block driven into the ground.
A diaphragm wall panel made with bentonite slurry support.
The reinforced concrete grillage tying the pile heads together.
A “transitional” solution between shallow and deep foundations, also called a well foundation in Hungarian practice.
For a wind turbine, what governs the design of the foundation?
The tilt of the tower: the allowable differential settlement is approx. 3 mm/m.
The chemical aggressiveness of the groundwater.
The weight of the blades.
The depth of frost penetration.
For tall, slender towers even a small differential settlement causes significant tilt.
What does the pile foundation of a new structure consist of?
The piles and the cap, slab and/or grillage tying their heads together.
Only the piles – the superstructure rests directly on them.
The piles and the grout injected around them.
A strip footing with a layer of replaced soil below it.
The connecting structure distributes the load and makes the piles work together.
Which is NOT a reason why more and more deep foundations are built today?
The standards no longer allow shallow foundations.
Buildings with ever larger loads and greater sensitivity to settlement are being built.
The sites with good subsoil have run out.
Deep foundation technologies have become competitive.
Shallow foundations are still fully accepted today – where suitable, they are often the cheapest.
Why is a bridge pier standing in a river bed placed on piles?
Because the scour hole around the pier can reach the base of a shallow foundation, whereas the piles reach below the scour depth.
Because the shallow foundation would float up due to buoyancy.
Because piles do not corrode in water.
Scour is one of the most common causes of bridge damage – that is why river piers get deep foundations.
The piles of the Burj Khalifa (828 m) are shorter than the foundation elements of the Petronas Towers (452 m). What is the main reason?
The depth of the foundation is set primarily by the subsoil, the depth of the bearing stratum.
A taller building is always lighter.
There is no groundwater in Dubai.
The Burj Khalifa was built on a diaphragm wall.
It is not the height of the building but the soil that decides how deep the foundation has to reach.

Infill site in the city centre

A six-storey office building is being built on a city-centre infill site; on both sides there are hundred-year-old apartment blocks sensitive to vibration. The sandy gravel bearing stratum is approx. 9 m deep.
Which piling technology is the riskiest here?
Driven precast reinforced concrete pile
Bored pile (CFA)
Displacement screw pile

Pile driving causes significant noise and vibration, so near structures it can only be used under strict limits – next to vibration-sensitive neighbours it is the riskiest. CFA is chosen specifically where noise and vibration are restricted, the screw pile has no dynamic effect or noise, and the micropile is made with a small rig, without vibration.
Underground car park on the site boundary

The excavation for a two-level underground car park has to be supported. The groundwater is 2 m below ground level, impermeable clay follows at a depth of 14 m, and old buildings stand directly on the site boundary.
Which structure would you choose?
A row of CFA piles
Gravel piles

The diaphragm wall is watertight and stiff, it is built relatively free of noise and vibration, no groundwater lowering is needed, and socketed into the impermeable clay it can also be the permanent side wall of the car park. A row of CFA piles does not keep out the water, the well foundation is a foundation and not excavation support, and the gravel pile is a ground improvement method.
Adding storeys to an old apartment block

Two storeys are being added to an old apartment block, and the existing strip footings can no longer carry the extra load. Work is only possible from the cellar, where the headroom is barely more than two metres.
How would you strengthen the foundations?
With micropile underpinning
With large-diameter cased piles
With Franki piles
With driven precast reinforced concrete piles

A micropile can be made even at a workplace with difficult access and limited headroom, and it transfers the loads of the existing foundations to the deeper, better layer (underpinning). Its base resistance is neglected, and in soft soil (c<sub>u</sub> < 10 kPa) buckling must also be checked. The other technologies need a large rig, and the vibration from driving and ramming would also damage the old building.
A bridge pier in the river bed
The river pier of a long-span road bridge has to be founded. The sandy gravel of the bed may be scoured in a flood, the reliable bearing stratum is 25–30 m deep, and the loads are large.
What is the most obvious solution today?
Large-diameter bentonite-supported bored piles
A shallow foundation on the river bed
Timber piles

Because of the risk of scour, a shallow foundation is out of the question here: a deep foundation is needed. For large-diameter, deep piles of high bearing capacity, the slurry-supported bored pile has become widespread – in Hungary mainly for the foundations of long-span bridges, precisely. The older Danube bridges in Budapest were still built on box foundations (caissons); this has been pushed out today.
A crane hall on flowing silt

A heavy hall with overhead cranes is being built. The top 25 m layer is flowing silt with a high water content, the groundwater is almost at the surface, and dense gravel lies below. Piles 120 cm in diameter and 30 m long are needed.
Which technology would you choose?
A cased bored pile
A CFA pile
An unsupported bored pile
A precast steel ground screw
A residential building on hard clay
Piles 7 m long and 60 cm in diameter are needed under a smaller residential building. The soil is hard cohesive clay throughout; the investigation found no groundwater even down to 15 m.
What is the simplest solution?
An unsupported bored pile, concreted immediately
A bentonite-supported bored pile
A caisson foundation

In cohesive soil, above the groundwater, to a depth of at most 8–10 m, the bore is stable for a short time even without support – but it must be concreted immediately after excavation. Slurry is an unnecessary cost here, and the caisson and the diaphragm wall are structures an order of magnitude larger.
A diaphragm wall into rock
The excavation of a metro station is enclosed by a 45 m deep diaphragm wall; the lower part of the wall goes into hard marl, rock.
What would you excavate the trench with?
With a hydrofraise (a trench cutter with cutter wheels)
With a rope-suspended mechanical grab
With a Kelly-bar hydraulic grab
Not at all: a driven steel sheet pile wall instead of a diaphragm wall

In rock or very hard clay a diaphragm wall can only be built with a hydrofraise: the cutter wheels break up the material, which is pumped out together with the slurry and then separated outside. It is very expensive, but it gives an accurate trench to great depth, in any soil and rock. In Hungary it was used for the construction of metro line 4: diaphragm walls 48.3 m deep at Fővám tér and 40 m deep at Szent Gellért tér. Sheet piles cannot be driven into rock.
A solar park on farmland
A solar park is being built with several thousand lightly loaded support posts. The soil is medium-dense sand, and the posts must be easy to remove decades later.
What would you found the posts on?
On large-diameter bored piles
On a diaphragm wall
On Franki piles

The ground screw is for founding lightly loaded structures – lightweight houses, solar parks, fences, mobile stands: it can be installed quickly and without vibration by machine (smaller ones even by hand), and it is recoverable, it can be unscrewed. It is typically at most 2–3 m long and works where it can cut a thread into the soil.
A hall for moderate loads is being built with several hundred piles. The soil is loose to medium-dense sand, removing the spoil would be expensive, and the work has to progress quickly.
Which technology fits here best?
A cast-in-place displacement screw pile
A cased large-diameter bored pile

The drilling head of the screw pile pushes aside and compacts the soil while drilling: the shaft resistance increases, only a little spoil comes to the surface, and there is no dynamic effect or noise. In loose to medium-dense granular and intermediate soils it is a popular, economical and fast solution for moderately loaded industrial facilities (diameter 300–600 mm, length up to approx. 20 m).
